hints: Start by thinking what gives a bacterial cell wall its strength, and what happens to water movement if that strength is lost in a growing cell.
Recall which enzyme makes the cross-links between peptidoglycan chains, and when those links are made during the cell cycle.
Look at Fig. 3.1 and trace the path penicillin would have to take to reach the thin peptidoglycan layer in E. coli compared with a Gram-positive cell.
walkthrough:
How penicillin weakens the wall**
Think of peptidoglycan as a mesh. Its strength comes from short peptide cross-links joining adjacent glycan chains. Those links are made by enzymes called transpeptidases when the cell is growing and making new wall.

Why the cell bursts**
Penicillin binds to and inhibits those transpeptidases, so new cross-links cannot form. The wall becomes weak. Water then enters by osmosis and the cell lyses because the weakened wall cannot resist the internal pressure.

Why Gram-negative cells are protected**
In Fig. 3.1 the peptidoglycan in E. coli is thin and sits underneath an extra outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide and porins. That outer membrane acts as a barrier that slows or blocks penicillin reaching the peptidoglycan. Proteins in the outer membrane can also pump penicillin out, and enzymes in the periplasm can break it down.

Final answer: Penicillin weakens the cell wall by inhibiting transpeptidase enzymes, preventing formation of cross-links between peptidoglycan chains in growing cells, leading to lysis. In Gram-negative E. coli the outer membrane prevents entry of penicillin to the peptidoglycan, and periplasmic enzymes / efflux pumps may degrade or remove it.

hints: Think about what active transport needs that diffusion and facilitated diffusion do not need.
walkthrough:
What passive means**
Passive movement happens down a concentration gradient using the kinetic energy of the molecules themselves. That means the cell does not have to supply ATP or any other metabolic energy to drive it.
Final answer: No ATP / no metabolic energy is required.

hints: Look at the shape of the porin in Fig. 3.1 spanning the outer membrane and think what general class of membrane protein forms an open passage.
Use the information that each OmpF is made from three identical polypeptides to think about levels of protein structure.
Remember that water, ions and small polar molecules cannot easily cross the hydrophobic fatty acid core, so think how the inside of the passage must be lined.
Link that open hydrophilic passage to the type of transport that increases membrane permeability without ATP.
walkthrough:
A channel, not a carrier**
The diagram shows OmpF spanning the outer membrane as an open tube. That is the hallmark of a channel protein or pore protein. It provides a continuous water-filled route, so solutes do not dissolve in the lipid bilayer.

Built from three parts**
One polypeptide is primary structure folded into secondary and tertiary structure. When three identical polypeptides assemble together to make one functional OmpF, that is quaternary structure.

Hydrophilic inside, hydrophobic outside**
The outside of the protein that contacts the fatty acid tails is hydrophobic. The amino acids lining the pore have hydrophilic R-groups, creating a hydrophilic water-filled channel. That lets polar molecules and ions bypass the hydrophobic barrier.

Facilitated diffusion for water**
Because the pore is open, movement is by facilitated diffusion down a concentration gradient with no ATP. This greatly increases permeability of the outer membrane to water and small polar solutes, allowing osmosis and ion movement.

Final answer: Channel / pore protein with quaternary structure formed from three polypeptides; hydrophilic R-groups line a water-filled pore allowing facilitated diffusion of water, ions and small polar molecules, increasing permeability for osmosis; globular protein with no specific binding site.

hints: Recall where protein synthesis happens and which codon on mRNA normally signals the start of that process.
Think what must physically attach at that START region for a polypeptide to begin, and what happens if micF is already covering it.
walkthrough:
Blocking the start signal**
To make OmpF, the ribosome must read the OmpF mRNA starting at the START codon, usually AUG. MicF is complementary to that region, so it binds over it and covers it up.

No initiation, no protein**
With the START region double-stranded and hidden, the mRNA cannot correctly attach to the small ribosomal subunit, and the first tRNA carrying methionine cannot pair with the START codon. Initiation of translation therefore fails and no new OmpF polypeptide chain is built.

Final answer: Translation of OmpF mRNA is blocked so polypeptide synthesis cannot occur; mRNA cannot attach to the ribosome / small subunit and the first tRNA carrying methionine cannot attach at the START codon.

hints: Break the word into poly- and saccharide and think what small sugar unit is repeated.
Think how those sugar units are joined together and what larger features such a chain can have.
walkthrough:
Many sugars joined**
Poly means many, so a polysaccharide is a large molecule made of many monosaccharide monomers, for example glucose residues, linked into a chain.

How they are linked**
Adjacent monomers are joined by glycosidic bonds made in condensation reactions with loss of water. The resulting polymer can be straight or branched, which is why the O antigen and core in Fig. 3.1 are drawn as chains of hexagons.
Final answer: A polymer / chain of many monosaccharide / sugar monomers joined by glycosidic bonds formed by condensation; may be branched or unbranched.

hints: Think about what part of the bacterium the immune system recognises, and whether that part is the same in different strains.
Recall which cells carry specific receptors that must match that shape before an immune response starts.
Think what happens after recovery in terms of memory cells, and whether those memory cells would match a new shape.
walkthrough:
Different antigens, different shapes**
The O polysaccharide acts as an antigen. Different pathogenic strains have O antigens built from different sugars, so the overall 3D shape is different.

Specific recognition**
B and T lymphocytes each carry receptors with one specific shape. An immune response only starts when a receptor binds its complementary antigen. So strain 1 will stimulate one set of lymphocytes to divide and secrete one specific antibody, while strain 2 needs a different set.

Memory does not cross-protect**
After the first infection, memory cells remain, but they are specific to the first O-antigen shape. They will not bind or respond rapidly to the different O-antigen of the second strain, so a new primary response is needed and there is no immunity.

Final answer: Different strains have different O-antigen shapes; B / T lymphocytes have specific receptors so only the matching antigen activates them to produce specific antibodies; memory cells formed to the first strain do not recognise a different O-antigen, so no secondary response.
